### Foundations

1. Teach reading and writing first, then arithmetic.
2. Use local materials, stories, and practical problems.

### Apprenticeship

1. Pair learners with skilled practitioners.
2. Progress from observation to supervised work to independent practice.

### Assessment

1. Check understanding with practical tasks.
2. Adjust instruction to close gaps.

## Safety Notes

- Safeguard children; keep learning environments safe and inclusive.

title: Library Organization
body:
## Overview

An organized library keeps knowledge findable for generations. A simple classification plus a catalog protects against loss and makes retrieval fast.

## Prerequisites

- None

## Materials & Tools

- Shelving
- Catalog cards or ledger
- Labels and ink

## Procedure

### Classification

1. Group by broad subject, then by author or title.
2. Assign a stable call number to every item.

### Catalog

1. Record title, author, subject, and location for each item.
2. Maintain an index for cross-referencing.

### Preservation

1. Keep collections dry, dark, and pest-free.
2. Copy fragile items and store masters separately.

## Safety Notes

- Control humidity and fire risk; back up catalogs.

title: Map Making
yield: A scaled sketch map of about 1 square kilometre with bearings, distances, water, and hazards
season: Survey in dry, clear weather; leaf cover and floods hide features in wet seasons
storage: Keep the master map flat, dry, and out of sunlight; store a digital copy separately
hazards: Exposure to heat, cold, and storms
lifespan: A local map remains useful for 5-10 years if updated
maintenance: Correct after new roads, bridges, or flood damage; recheck declination yearly
limits: A sketch map is not a legal property survey
Magnetic bearings must be corrected for declination
Do not enter restricted or unsafe areas without permission

sources.title: US Army FM 21-26 Map Reading and Land Navigation
International Cartographic Association Map Design Guidance

body:
## Overview

A useful map records what a traveler needs: distance, direction, water, hazards,
and landmarks. You do not need a survey-grade instrument. A compass, a measured
baseline, pacing, and a consistent symbol set can produce a sketch map accurate
enough for route planning, disaster response, and local records.

## Prerequisites

- Compass and pace-count skills
- Basic arithmetic and scale drawing

## Materials & Tools

- Compass with adjustable declination
- Measuring tape or rope for a baseline
- Graph paper, clipboard, pencil, and eraser
- GPS or phone for checkpoints
- Range poles or flags
- Clinometer or phone level for slopes
- Waterproof map case

## Procedure

### 1. Set the scale and orientation

1. Decide the area and the smallest feature to show; choose a scale such as
   1:2,000 for a village or 1:50,000 for a district.
2. Draw a north arrow and note magnetic declination.
3. Mark a known baseline on the ground and measure it twice.
4. Establish two fixed reference points that will not move.

### 2. Survey by bearing and distance

1. From each reference point, take bearings to corners, buildings, wells, and
   road junctions.
2. Measure or pace each distance; calibrate your pace over 100 m first.
3. Plot each point by drawing a line along its bearing and marking the scaled
   distance.
4. Use triangulation from two known points to locate features you cannot reach.

### 3. Add terrain and symbols

1. Sketch contours from slope breaks and spot heights, or use a GPS track.
2. Mark water, seasonal streams, flood lines, bridges, and steep grades.
3. Use a legend with consistent symbols for buildings, fields, roads, and
   hazards.
4. Add a title, date, scale bar, north arrow, and surveyor's name.

### 4. Check and reproduce

1. Walk the map with a local guide and correct errors in the field.
2. Compare distances and bearings at several checkpoints.
3. Copy the final map in ink or scan it; store a master away from the field
   copy.
4. Record magnetic declination and the date, since it changes slowly.

## Safety Notes

- **Green hazard:** Field mapping is low risk, but traffic, weather, and
  trespassing are real concerns. Ask permission and avoid restricted areas.
- Do not rely on a phone battery alone; carry a compass and paper map.
- River crossings and steep ground require a partner and a turn-around time.
- A sketch map is not a legal property survey.

title: Measurement & Records
body:
## Overview

Consistent measurement and record-keeping make knowledge reproducible. Standard units, calibrated references, and ledgers underpin trade and science.

## Prerequisites

- None

## Materials & Tools

- Standard weights and measures
- Ledger or logbook
- Calibration references

## Procedure

### Standards

1. Adopt units for length, mass, volume, and time.
2. Keep master references under protection.

### Records

1. Log observations with date, method, and conditions.
2. Cross-reference entries for auditability.

## Safety Notes

- Guard standards against wear and tampering.

title: Music
body:
## Overview

Music is a universal human language. It binds communities, transmits stories,
and heals trauma. Instruments can be built from local materials.

## Prerequisites

- [Simple Tools](../survival/simple-tools.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Wood, gut, hide, bamboo, gourd
- Metal (for strings, bells)
- Voice

## Procedure

### Rhythm First

1. Clapping patterns: 4/4, 3/4, 6/8.
2. Call and response.
3. Polyrhythms: two patterns at once.

### Drums

- **Frame drum:** hide stretched over a wooden hoop.
- **Djembe:** goblet-shaped, rope-tuned.
- **Log drum:** hollowed log with slits.

### Jaw Harp

1. Shape a metal or bamboo tongue in a frame.
2. Pluck the tongue while changing mouth shape.
3. Mouth cavity amplifies harmonics.

### Flutes

- **Bamboo flute:** cut a tube, bore finger holes, notch the mouthpiece.
- **Pan pipes:** graduated tubes bound together.
- **Ocarina:** closed vessel with finger holes.

### String Instruments

- **Berimbau:** bow with a gourd resonator.
- **Lyre:** U-shaped frame with strings.
- **Guitar:** box with neck and frets.

### Music Theory (Basic)

1. **Scale:** 7 notes per octave (do re mi fa sol la ti).
2. **Intervals:** distance between notes.
3. **Chords:** three or more notes together.
4. **Keys:** major (bright), minor (dark).

### Singing

1. Breathe from the diaphragm.
2. Open the throat.
3. Match pitch with an instrument.
4. Sing in rounds, harmonies, and unison.

### Songs for Community

- Work songs (rhythm for shared labor).
- Lullabies.
- Lamentations.
- Celebration songs.
- Anthems.

### Recording (If Available)

- Wax cylinder, magnetic tape, or digital.
- Preserve for future generations.

## Safety Notes

- Green — but loud sounds damage hearing. Protect ears around drums.
- Singing is safe; hydrate.

title: Optics
body:
## Overview

Optics magnify, focus, and direct light, enabling reading aids, telescopes, microscopes, and fire-starting. Grinding and polishing produce lenses from glass.

## Prerequisites

- Glass Making

## Materials & Tools

- Glass blanks
- Abrasives and pitch
- Polishing rouge

## Procedure

### Grinding

1. Rough-grind the blank against a tool with coarse abrasive.
2. Progress to finer abrasives until the curve is correct.

### Polishing

1. Polish on pitch with rouge until clear.
2. Test focus on a bright object.

### Use

1. Combine lenses into a telescope or microscope.
2. Focus sunlight for ignition.

## Safety Notes

- Never view the sun directly through optics; it causes blindness.
- Focused sunlight can start fires instantly.

title: Oral History
body:
## Overview

When writing is scarce, oral history preserves memory, law, and craft. Structured interviews and mnemonic devices keep it accurate.

## Prerequisites

- None

## Materials & Tools

- Notebook or recording device
- Question guides
- Storytellers

## Procedure

### Collecting

1. Interview elders with open questions and permission.
2. Record exact wording and context.

### Preserving

1. Transcribe and cross-check with other accounts.
2. Teach key stories to younger people through repetition and song.

## Safety Notes

- Obtain consent and respect cultural ownership of stories.

title: Printing
body:
## Overview

Printing spreads knowledge cheaply and durably. Movable type, an oil ink, and a screw press let a small community reproduce books and posters.

## Prerequisites

- Paper Making

## Materials & Tools

- Movable metal or wooden type
- Oil-based ink
- Screw press
- Paper

## Procedure

### Making Type

1. Carve or cast reversed letters at a uniform height.
2. Sort type into a case by frequency.

### Setting & Inking

1. Compose text in a galley, locked into a forme.
2. Ink the forme evenly with leather balls or a roller.

### Pressing

1. Lay paper, close the tympan, and run the press.
2. Hang sheets to dry; print the second side after drying.

## Safety Notes

- Ink and solvent fumes require ventilation.
- Keep hands clear of the press platen.

title: Radio

sources.title: US Army Signal Corps manuals (public domain)

body:
## Overview

Radio links communities beyond line of sight, using no infrastructure. A simple crystal set receives; a low-power transceiver sends voice or Morse.

## Prerequisites

- Electrical Wiring

## Materials & Tools

- Copper wire
- Variable capacitor and coil
- Crystal earpiece or diode
- Antenna wire

## Procedure

### Receiver

1. Wind a coil and connect it to a variable capacitor to tune.
2. Add a diode detector and crystal earpiece.
3. Connect a long wire antenna and a good earth.

### Antenna

1. Run a half-wave dipole as high and clear as possible.
2. Feed with twin lead or coax and seal connections.

### Transmission

1. Use low power and a licensed band.
2. Send Morse or voice; identify your station.

## Safety Notes

- Powerful transmitters and antennas can cause RF burns and shocks.
- Follow local spectrum rules and keep emergency frequencies clear.

title: Teaching Literacy
yield: A 12-week small-group sequence taking non-readers through letter sounds, blending, and short sentences
season: Run in the off-season or evening; keep sessions short and regular
storage: Keep lesson cards, readers, and learner records dry and organised
hazards: Learner dropout from embarrassment or punishment

resourceBudget.batch: one class of 10 learners for 12 weeks

lifespan: A lesson sequence remains usable for 1-3 years with revision
maintenance: Review assessments each term and replace worn cards and readers
limits: Not a substitute for trained teachers in formal certification
Do not use corporal punishment or public shaming
Adapt examples and orthography to the local language

sources.title: RTI International Early Grade Reading Guidance

body:
## Overview

Literacy teaching works best as a short, regular routine: hear sounds, connect
them to letters, blend words, read a short text, and write a sentence. Learners
need practice at the right level, not a lecture about grammar. A community
teacher can run a small group with a chalkboard, paper, and a simple sequence.

## Prerequisites

- Fluency in the language of instruction
- A quiet space and regular meeting time

## Materials & Tools

- Chalkboard or large paper
- Letter cards and word cards
- Decodable readers or short local texts
- Notebooks and pencils
- Assessment sheet
- Picture cards for vocabulary
- Timer or bell

## Procedure

### 1. Build oral language and sounds

1. Start with familiar words, names, and local stories.
2. Clap syllables and isolate first and last sounds.
3. Teach one or two letter-sound pairs at a time; review previous ones daily.
4. Use pictures and actions to anchor new vocabulary.

### 2. Connect sounds to print

1. Show the letter, say its sound, and have learners trace it in sand or on
   paper.
2. Blend sounds into words: /m/ /a/ /p/ becomes "map".
3. Build words with letter cards and change one sound at a time.
4. Read the word aloud, then have each learner read it individually.

### 3. Read and write a short text

1. Use a decodable text that contains only taught sounds and a few new words.
2. Read together, then in pairs, then silently.
3. Ask two comprehension questions: who, what, where, or why.
4. Finish with a dictated sentence or a personal sentence using a new word.

### 4. Assess and regroup

1. Check letter sounds, word reading, and a short writing sample every few weeks.
2. Group learners by the skill they need, not by age.
3. Give extra practice to those who are stuck; do not move on too quickly.
4. Celebrate progress and keep a simple record for each learner.

## Safety Notes

- **Green hazard:** Teaching is low risk, but classrooms still need safe exits,
  clean water, and protection from weather.
- Never use corporal punishment or public humiliation; they drive learners away.
- Adapt examples to the local language and culture.
- Protect learner records and privacy.

title: Adhesives
yield: About 1 kg of usable starch, hide, or casein glue, enough for several small joints
season: Make in dry, moderate weather; damp cold slows curing
storage: Keep dry ingredients sealed; refrigerate starch paste and discard after a few days
hazards: Burns from hot glue and double boilers
Caustic burns from lime or borax
Mould growth in starch and hide glues
lifespan: Dry hide glue keeps for years; starch paste lasts only days
maintenance: Make fresh paste, label batches, and test each new glue batch on scrap
limits: Starch and hide glues are not waterproof
Casein is water-resistant but not a structural adhesive for safety-critical loads
Do not use unknown adhesives on food or drinking-water contact surfaces

sources.title: Canadian Conservation Institute Adhesives and Consolidants

body:
## Overview

Simple adhesives can be made from starch, hide, milk protein, and lime. Each
has a different strength, water resistance, and working time. The joint usually
fails because the surfaces are dirty, the fit is poor, or the glue is too thick;
surface preparation matters more than the recipe.

## Prerequisites

- Measuring by weight
- Basic heating and woodworking skills

## Materials & Tools

- Wheat or cassava starch
- Hide glue granules or sheets
- Casein powder or skim milk
- Slaked lime or borax as required by the recipe
- Clean water
- Sandpaper and a stiff brush
- Heat source and double boiler
- Scales, cups, and a stirring stick
- Clamps and scrap wood for test joints

## Procedure

### 1. Prepare the surfaces

1. Remove dust, oil, old glue, and loose fibres.
2. Roughen smooth surfaces slightly and dry them.
3. Test the fit; a gap thicker than about 0.2 mm weakens most natural glues.
4. Warm the room and the parts; cold surfaces shorten working time.

### 2. Make starch paste

1. Mix one part starch with enough cold water to make a smooth slurry.
2. Add about five parts hot water while stirring, then heat gently until the
   mixture turns clear and thick.
3. Stir out lumps and thin with water if needed; the paste should spread like
   thick cream.
4. Use while warm; starch paste has a short working life and is not waterproof.

### 3. Make hide glue

1. Soak hide glue in water until soft, then heat it gently in a double boiler.
2. Do not boil; overheating degrades the protein and weakens the joint.
3. Adjust water to reach a syrupy consistency and skim any foam.
4. Apply warm, clamp firmly, and leave overnight.

### 4. Make casein glue

1. Follow a tested recipe that combines casein, water, and a small amount of
   alkali such as slaked lime or borax.
2. Mix to a smooth paste and let it stand briefly before use.
3. Apply a thin even coat, clamp, and keep the joint dry while it cures.
4. Test on scrap before using on a finished piece.

## Safety Notes

- **Yellow hazard:** Hot glue and caustic lime can cause burns. Wear gloves and
  eye protection.
- Hide glue and starch can grow mould; keep containers clean and discard spoiled
  batches.
- Use casein in a ventilated area and avoid inhaling powder.
- Do not use unknown adhesives on food containers, water pipes, or medical
  items.

title: Blacksmithing
body:
## Overview

Blacksmithing shapes wrought iron and steel by heating and hammering. It
produces tools, weapons, hardware, and fasteners.

## Prerequisites

- [Charcoal Production](charcoal-production.md)
- [Metal Smelting](metal-smelting.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Forge (clay or steel)
- Anvil (or dense stone)
- Hammer (2–4 kg)
- Tongs
- Quench tank (oil or water)
- Charcoal

## Procedure

### Setting Up the Forge

1. Build a clay hearth with a tuyere at the center.
2. Connect bellows or blower.
3. Fill with charcoal; light from the top.
4. Air blast raises temp to 1,200–1,400°C.

### Basic Forging

1. Heat metal to bright orange-yellow (1,100°C).
2. Remove; hammer immediately.
3. Reheat as it turns cherry red (below 800°C).
4. Shape by drawing, upsetting, bending, or punching.

### Drawing Out

1. Heat a section.
2. Hammer on the anvil's horn or face, striking perpendicular to length.
3. Rotate 90° between blows to keep square.

### Upsetting

1. Heat the end.
2. Strike downward onto the anvil; thickness increases, length shortens.

### Welding (Forge Weld)

1. Heat both pieces to white-yellow (1,300°C).
2. Sprinkle borax as flux.
3. Overlap; hammer rapidly. The pieces fuse.

### Heat Treatment

1. **Annealing:** heat to red, cool slowly in ash.
2. **Normalizing:** heat to red, air-cool.
3. **Hardening:** heat to red, quench in oil or water.
4. **Tempering:** reheat to 200–300°C (straw to purple color), then cool.

## Safety Notes

- **Red hazard:** Burns, eye injuries, and hearing damage are common.
- Wear leather apron, eye protection, ear protection.
- Never quench in water without knowing the steel — cracking risk.
- Keep water away from the forge unless intentional.
- Ventilate for CO.

title: Brick Making
materialsRequired: Clay (test: rolls into a smooth snake without cracking)
body:
## Overview

Bricks are clay fired to hardness. They are the backbone of durable
construction — houses, kilns, furnaces, chimneys.

## Prerequisites

- [Making Fire](../survival/making-fire.md)
- [Charcoal Production](charcoal-production.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Clay (test: rolls into a smooth snake without cracking)
- Sand (temper)
- Water
- Wooden molds
- Kiln or clamp

## Procedure

### Clay Preparation

1. Dig clay; remove rocks and roots.
2. Add sand (10–20% by volume) to reduce shrinkage.
3. Add water; knead to plastic consistency.
4. Let rest 24 hours (aging improves workability).

### Molding

1. Wet mold; dust with sand.
2. Press clay firmly into mold.
3. Strike off excess with a board.
4. Turn out onto a drying board.

### Drying

1. Air-dry in shade 1–2 weeks.
2. Turn daily to prevent warping.
3. Bone-dry before firing (no moisture).

### Firing

1. Build a clamp: stack bricks with gaps for fire.
2. Cover with mud; leave air channels at base.
3. Fire slowly for 24 hours; peak at 900–1,000°C.
4. Cool 2 days before opening.

### Testing

- Fired brick rings when struck.
- Underfired brick is dull and crumbles.
- Overfired brick is glassy and vitrified (good for kilns).

## Safety Notes

- **Yellow hazard:** Silica dust in clay — wear mask when dry mixing.
- Firing clamp releases smoke and CO — keep away from dwellings.
- Do not use bricks from unknown sources for food-contact surfaces.

title: Ceramics
yield: About 8-15 food-safe vessels from a 20 kg clay batch after drying and firing losses
season: Dig clay in dry weather; fire after the wet season when fuel and pots are dry
storage: Store clay damp and covered; keep glaze materials labelled and away from food
hazards: Crystalline silica dust from clay and glazes
Lead or heavy-metal poisoning from unsafe glazes
lifespan: Properly fired stoneware can last for decades
maintenance: Inspect kiln elements, shelves, and vents every firing; re-level shelves seasonally
limits: Never fire wet or thick uneven ware
Do not use lead glazes on food-contact surfaces
Test clay shrinkage and glaze fit before making a full batch

sources.title: The Potter's Dictionary of Materials and Techniques
American Ceramic Society Firing and Glazing Guides

body:
## Overview

Ceramics turn clay into containers, tiles, filters, and refractory parts that
survive heat and moisture. The craft is mostly control: consistent clay, slow
drying, and a firing curve matched to the body and glaze. Most failures come
from wet or uneven pieces, soluble salts, or a glaze that does not fit the clay.

## Prerequisites

- Clay source and water
- Kiln or pit-firing experience
- Safe handling of dust and heat

## Materials & Tools

- Clay body and temper (sand, grog, or crushed fired clay)
- Water and a clean mixing surface
- Plaster bats or boards for drying
- Kiln shelves, posts, and cones
- Lead-free glaze materials
- Dust mask, eye protection, and heat-resistant gloves
- Buckets, sieve, and scales

## Procedure

### 1. Test the clay

1. Dig or buy clay and remove stones and roots.
2. Make small test tiles and measure drying and firing shrinkage.
3. Add temper if the clay cracks or is too plastic; mix thoroughly and age it
   for several days.
4. Fire a test tile to the intended temperature before committing a batch.

### 2. Form and dry

1. Wedge the clay to remove air pockets and even out moisture.
2. Form by pinching, coiling, slabs, or a wheel; keep joins damp and score them.
3. Dry slowly under cloth or plastic, away from sun and drafts, until leather
   hard and then bone dry.
4. Do not fire a piece that still feels cool or heavy with moisture.

### 3. Bisque fire

1. Load shelves with adequate spacing and support each piece evenly.
2. Fire slowly through the water-smoking stage, then raise to the bisque
   temperature recommended for the clay.
3. Cool the kiln slowly; rapid cooling can crack ware.
4. Inspect for cracks and sand rough edges before glazing.

### 4. Glaze and fire

1. Use lead-free glazes for anything that will touch food.
2. Apply an even coat, keep glaze off kiln shelves, and clean the foot ring.
3. Fire to the glaze maturity temperature with cones visible through the peep
   hole.
4. Test finished ware for crazing, leaching, and thermal shock before daily use.

## Safety Notes

- **Yellow hazard:** Clay and glaze dust contain crystalline silica. Mix wet,
  wear a respirator, and never dry-sweep the work area.
- Kilns reach over 1,000 C and can cause severe burns; use gloves, tongs, and a
  clear cool-down period.
- Fuel kilns produce carbon monoxide. Fire outdoors or in a ventilated space
  with a carbon monoxide alarm.
- Lead glazes are a serious poisoning risk, especially for children. Use
  lead-free recipes and test food-contact surfaces.

title: Charcoal Production
body:
## Overview

Charcoal burns hotter and cleaner than wood and is essential for smelting
and blacksmithing. It is made by pyrolysis — burning wood with limited oxygen.

## Prerequisites

- [Making Fire](../survival/making-fire.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Hardwood (oak, hickory, mesquite)
- Earth or sand
- Shovel
- Water (for quenching)

## Procedure

### Earth Kiln Method

1. Clear a 2 m circle; level the ground.
2. Stack hardwood in a dome, leaving a central chimney.
3. Cover the pile with leaves, then earth, leaving the chimney open.
4. Light the chimney.
5. When smoke turns from white to blue, close the chimney.
6. Tend for 3–7 days, patching cracks as they appear.
7. When smoke stops, wait 24 hours; then open and quench with water.

### Retort Method (Higher Yield)

1. Place wood in a sealed metal drum.
2. Heat from outside; volatile gases escape via a pipe.
3. Those gases can fuel the fire — self-sustaining once started.
4. Cool before opening.

### Yield

- Earth kiln: 10–20% by weight
- Retort: 25–35%

### Uses

- Smelting iron, copper
- Blacksmithing forges
- Water filtration (activated charcoal)
- Gunpowder (see [Chemistry](chemistry.md))
- Medicinal (charcoal slurry for poisoning)

## Safety Notes

- **Yellow hazard:** Carbon monoxide from smoldering charcoal kills without warning. Work outdoors.
- Never seal a drum while hot — pressure builds.
- Quench thoroughly; buried embers can reignite days later.

title: Chemistry
materialsRequired: Acids: vinegar (acetic), citric (lemon), sulfuric (from sulfide ores)
Bases: lime (CaO), wood ash (K₂CO₃), ammonia (from urine)
body:
## Overview

Chemistry underpins soap, medicine, metallurgy, and agriculture. This entry
covers the foundational reactions and safety rules needed to produce acids,
bases, salts, and simple organic compounds.

## Prerequisites

- [Metal Smelting](metal-smelting.md)
- [Charcoal Production](charcoal-production.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Glass vessels (see [Glass Making](glass-making.md))
- Heat source (charcoal forge)
- Acids: vinegar (acetic), citric (lemon), sulfuric (from sulfide ores)
- Bases: lime (CaO), wood ash (K₂CO₃), ammonia (from urine)
- Litmus or red cabbage indicator

## Procedure

### Safety First

1. Always add acid to water, never water to acid.
2. Wear eye protection and gloves.
3. Work outdoors or under a fume hood.
4. Have a bucket of water and baking soda within reach.

### Making Sulfuric Acid (Lead Chamber)

1. Burn sulfur in a lead-lined chamber with moist air.
2. SO₂ + O₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₄.
3. Collect the acid at the chamber base.
4. Concentrate by boiling off water.

### Making Nitric Acid (Saltpeter + Sulfuric)

1. Mix saltpeter (KNO₃) with sulfuric acid in a glass retort.
2. Heat gently; distill nitric acid into a cooled receiver.
3. Store in dark glass.

### Making Hydrochloric Acid (Salt + Sulfuric)

1. Mix table salt with sulfuric acid.
2. Collect HCl gas in water.
3. Store in glass.

### Making Lye (Potassium Hydroxide)

1. Leach hardwood ash with rainwater.
2. Evaporate to concentrate.
3. Test with a fresh egg — it floats when strong enough.

### Making Soap (Saponification)

See [Soap Making](../survival/soap-making.md).

### Making Gunpowder

1. Mix 75% potassium nitrate, 15% charcoal, 10% sulfur by weight.
2. Mill to a fine powder.
3. **Red hazard:** Static sparks ignite powder. Work with wooden tools, ground yourself.

### pH Testing (Red Cabbage Indicator)

1. Boil red cabbage; save the purple liquid.
2. Add a drop of test solution.
3. Red = acid, green = base, purple = neutral.

### Common Reactions

- **Neutralization:** acid + base → salt + water.
- **Oxidation:** metal + oxygen → oxide.
- **Reduction:** oxide + carbon → metal + CO₂.
- **Combustion:** fuel + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O.

## Safety Notes

- **Red hazard:** Concentrated acids and bases destroy tissue on contact.
- **Red hazard:** Many reactions produce toxic or explosive gases.
- Never taste or smell chemicals directly.
- Never store acids in metal containers.
- Ventilate always.

title: Glass Making
materialsRequired: Soda ash (from burnt kelp or natron)
body:
## Overview

Glass is made from silica (sand), soda ash, and lime, melted at 1,400°C.
It is essential for windows, lenses, containers, and labware.

## Prerequisites

- [Charcoal Production](charcoal-production.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Silica sand (white, clean)
- Soda ash (from burnt kelp or natron)
- Lime (from limestone)
- Crucible (clay)
- Blowpipe
- Annealing oven

## Procedure

### Glass Batch

1. Mix by weight: 70% silica, 15% soda ash, 10% lime, 5% cullet (recycled glass).
2. Grind to powder; mix thoroughly.

### Melting

1. Heat crucible in furnace to 1,400°C.
2. Add batch slowly; it will foam as CO₂ escapes.
3. Skim off impurities.
4. Hold at 1,200°C for working.

### Blowing

1. Dip blowpipe in molten glass; gather a gob.
2. Roll on a marver (metal plate) to shape.
3. Blow gently through the pipe; rotate continuously.
4. Shape with jacks (tongs) and a wooden paddle.
5. Transfer to a punty rod for the open end.

### Annealing

1. Place finished glass in an oven at 500°C.
2. Cool slowly (1°C/min) to room temperature.
3. Rapid cooling causes shattering.

### Flat Glass (Cylinder Method)

1. Blow a large cylinder.
2. Cut off ends; slit lengthwise.
3. Reheat and flatten in an oven.

## Safety Notes

- **Red hazard:** Molten glass causes severe burns and sticks to skin.
- Furnace gases (CO, SO₂) are toxic — ventilate.
- Silica dust causes silicosis — wear respirator when mixing batch.
- Never quench hot glass in water.

title: Leather Tanning
body:
## Overview

Tanning stabilizes animal hide against rot. Methods: vegetable (bark),
brain, alum, and chrome. Vegetable is the safest and most traditional.

## Prerequisites

- [Raising Livestock](../agriculture/raising-livestock.md)
- [Simple Tools](../survival/simple-tools.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Fresh hide
- Bark (oak, chestnut, mimosa — high tannin)
- Lime (for dehairing)
- Fleshing knife
- Tanning vat
- Wooden beam

## Procedure

### Fleshing

1. Soak the hide in water 1–2 days.
2. Lay over a beam; scrape flesh and fat with a dull knife.
3. Remove hair by soaking in lime water (pH 12) 1–2 weeks.
4. Scrape hair and epidermis.

### Deliming & Bating

1. Rinse in water.
2. Soak in a weak acid (vinegar or bran water) 1 day to neutralize lime.
3. Bate (soften) in a warm manure or enzyme solution 1–3 days.

### Vegetable Tanning

1. Build a series of vats with increasing tannin concentration.
2. Start with weak "spent" tan liquor (1:10 bark to water).
3. Move the hide through stronger liquors over 4–12 weeks.
4. Finish in a strong tan pit 1–4 weeks.
5. When fully tanned (uniform brown throughout), remove.

### Brain Tanning (Native American Method)

1. Every animal has enough brain to tan its own hide.
2. Mash brain with water; work into the hide.
3. Stretch and dry; work with hands and a rope to soften.

### Finishing

1. Rinse.
2. Oil with tallow or fish oil.
3. Stretch and dry slowly.
4. Work with a slicker and stake to soften.
5. Smoke over a smoldering fire for color and water resistance.

## Safety Notes

- **Yellow hazard:** Lime burns skin; wear gloves and eye protection.
- Raw hides carry zoonotic diseases (anthrax, brucellosis) — handle with care.
- Tanning solutions smell; work outdoors, away from dwellings.

title: Lime & Cement

sources.title: US Bureau of Mines cement reports

body:
## Overview

Lime and cement are binders for masonry and concrete. Lime comes from
limestone (CaCO₃) burned to quicklime (CaO). Cement adds silica and alumina.

## Prerequisites

- [Brick Making](brick-making.md)
- [Charcoal Production](charcoal-production.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Limestone or chalk
- Kiln
- Water
- Sand, gravel (aggregate)
- Pozzolan (volcanic ash or fired clay)

## Procedure

### Lime Burning

1. Crush limestone to 5 cm pieces.
2. Fill kiln; fire to 900–1,000°C for 12–24 hours.
3. Quicklime (CaO) results — highly caustic.
4. Store in sealed containers away from moisture.

### Slaking

1. Slowly add water to quicklime (violent exotherm).
2. Result is slaked lime (Ca(OH)₂) — putty or powder.
3. Let mature 1–4 weeks before use.

### Lime Mortar

1. Mix 1 part lime putty to 3 parts sand.
2. Add water to workable consistency.
3. Use within 2 hours.
4. Cures by carbonation (absorbs CO₂) — slow, months.

### Hydraulic Lime

1. Limestone with 10–20% clay fires to hydraulic lime.
2. Sets underwater — useful for foundations and cisterns.

### Roman Cement (Pozzolanic)

1. Mix slaked lime with pozzolan (volcanic ash) 2:1.
2. Add sand and aggregate.
3. Sets hard underwater — used in aqueducts and harbors.

### Portland Cement (Modern)

1. Burn limestone + clay at 1,450°C to clinker.
2. Grind clinker with 5% gypsum to powder.
3. Mix with sand, gravel, water (1:2:3 by volume) for concrete.
4. Cure 28 days for full strength.

## Safety Notes

- **Red hazard:** Quicklime burns skin and eyes on contact; slaking releases
  boiling water. Wear full PPE.
- Cement dust causes silicosis and chemical burns — respirator, gloves.
- Never add water to cement in a confined space (heat and steam).

title: Metal Smelting
materialsRequired: Ore (malachite for copper; hematite/magnetite for iron)
body:
## Overview

Smelting extracts metal from ore using heat and a reducing agent (charcoal).
Start with copper (1,085°C), then bronze (alloy), then iron (1,538°C).

## Prerequisites

- [Charcoal Production](charcoal-production.md)
- [Simple Tools](../survival/simple-tools.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Ore (malachite for copper; hematite/magnetite for iron)
- Charcoal
- Clay furnace or bloomery
- Bellows
- Hammer and anvil

## Procedure

### Finding Ore

- **Copper:** green-stained rocks (malachite, azurite).
- **Iron:** red-brown rocks (hematite), magnetic black sand (magnetite).
- **Lead:** galena (gray cubic crystals).
- **Tin:** cassiterite (heavy black grains in stream beds).

### Building a Furnace

1. Build a clay cylinder 50 cm tall, 30 cm diameter.
2. Add a tuyere (air pipe) at the base for bellows.
3. Line with clay; let dry slowly.

### Copper Smelting

1. Crush ore to 1 cm pieces.
2. Layer charcoal and ore in furnace.
3. Light; pump bellows continuously.
4. After 45 min, tap slag; collect molten copper at base.
5. Yield: 5–20% copper by ore weight.

### Iron Bloomery

1. Same furnace, taller (1 m).
2. Alternate charcoal and crushed iron ore.
3. Pump bellows for 4–6 hours.
4. Extract a "bloom" — spongy iron mixed with slag.
5. Hammer the bloom while hot to expel slag (wrought iron).

### Bronze (Alloy)

1. Melt copper (1,085°C).
2. Add tin (10–12% by weight).
3. Cast into molds. Bronze is harder than copper and easier to cast.

### Cast Iron

1. Higher carbon content (2–4%).
2. Requires higher temp (1,200°C+) and continuous blast.
3. Brittle but hard; cast into shapes.

## Safety Notes

- **Red hazard:** Molten metal causes severe burns. Wear leather and eye protection.
- Metal fumes (lead, zinc, arsenic) are toxic — ventilate.
- Never pour molten metal onto wet surfaces (steam explosion).
- Carbon monoxide from charcoal — work outdoors.

title: Mills
materialsRequired: Wood for frame, gears, and wheel
body:
## Overview

Mills grind grain, press oil, saw wood, and full cloth. They are powered by
water, wind, or animals. Mills are force multipliers for any community.

## Prerequisites

- [Simple Tools](../survival/simple-tools.md)
- [Rope & Cordage](../survival/rope-cordage.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Millstones (hard granite or basalt)
- Wood for frame, gears, and wheel
- Metal bearings and shafts (see [Blacksmithing](blacksmithing.md))
- Water source or wind exposure

## Procedure

### Water Mill (Undershot)

1. Site on a stream with year-round flow.
2. Build a wheel 2–4 m diameter with paddles.
3. Mount on a horizontal axle; support with wooden or metal bearings.
4. Couple to millstone via gears (see [Mechanics](../materials/mechanics.md)).
5. Build a sluice to direct water onto the paddles.

### Water Mill (Overshot — More Efficient)

1. Build a flume to carry water over the top of the wheel.
2. Wheel has buckets instead of paddles.
3. Water weight drives the wheel downward.

### Windmill

1. Tower 6–12 m tall with a rotating top (cap).
2. Sails: 4 arms, 5–8 m each, covered with cloth or slats.
3. Tail pole or fantail keeps sails facing the wind.
4. Gearing drives millstone or pump.

### Animal Mill

1. Central post; horizontal beam.
2. Animal (ox, horse) walks in a circle.
3. Beam turns a vertical shaft connected to the millstone.

### Millstone Dressing

1. Cut grooves in a pattern (harps, quarter dress) to shear grain.
2. Sharpen every 100 hours of use.
3. Gap between stones: 0.3–0.6 mm for flour.

## Safety Notes

- **Yellow hazard:** Rotating shafts and gears cause entanglement. Guard them.
- Mill dust is explosive — ventilate.
- Millstones can shatter; never over-speed.
- Hearing protection near working mills.

title: Natural Dyes
materialsRequired: Mordant: alum, iron (rusty nails), copper, tannin
Large pot (enamel or stainless — never aluminum for mordanting)
body:
## Overview

Natural dyes color textiles, leather, and paper. Most require a mordant
(metal salt) to fix the color to fiber.

## Prerequisites

- [Rope & Cordage](../survival/rope-cordage.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Plant materials (see table)
- Mordant: alum, iron (rusty nails), copper, tannin
- Large pot (enamel or stainless — never aluminum for mordanting)
- Heat source

## Procedure

### Common Dye Plants

| Color | Source |
|-------|--------|
| Yellow | Onion skin, turmeric, marigold, chamomile |
| Orange | Carrot tops, safflower |
| Red | Madder root, cochineal (insect), beet (poor fastness) |
| Blue | Indigo, woad |
| Green | Overdye yellow with indigo |
| Brown | Walnut hulls, tea, coffee |
| Black | Oak gall + iron mordant |
| Purple | Logwood + iron, elderberry |

### Mordanting

1. Dissolve 10% alum (by fiber weight) in hot water.
2. Soak clean fiber 1 hour at 80°C.
3. Cool; rinse.

### Dyeing

1. Chop plant material; simmer 1 hour.
2. Strain; add wet, mordanted fiber.
3. Simmer 1 hour; stir gently.
4. Cool overnight in the dye bath.
5. Rinse until water runs clear.

### Modifying Color

- Add iron (rusty nails) → darkens, "saddens" colors.
- Add copper → shifts greens.
- Add vinegar → brightens reds.
- Add wood ash → shifts blues.

### Indigo (Vat Dyeing)

1. Ferment indigo with urine or lye + fructose.
2. Dip fiber; it appears yellow-green in the vat.
3. Expose to air; it oxidizes to blue.
4. Repeat dips for deeper blue.

## Safety Notes

- **Yellow hazard:** Mordants are metal salts — some (chromium, tin) are toxic.
  Use alum, iron, or copper only.
- Never use aluminum pots for dyeing or mordanting.
- Ventilate when simmering dye plants (some are allergenic).
- Some plants (pokeweed, bloodroot) are toxic; do not handle without gloves.

title: Paper Making
materialsRequired: Fiber: linen rag, cotton, hemp, straw
Mold and deckle (wooden frame with mesh)
body:
## Overview

Paper preserves knowledge. It is made from cellulose fiber (rag, hemp, straw)
beaten into pulp, then pressed and dried.

## Prerequisites

- [Rope & Cordage](../survival/rope-cordage.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Fiber: linen rag, cotton, hemp, straw
- Water
- Wooden beater or mortar
- Mold and deckle (wooden frame with mesh)
- Press
- Sizing (gelatin or starch)

## Procedure

### Preparing Pulp

1. Cut rags into 2 cm squares.
2. Ret in water 24 hours.
3. Beat with a wooden mallet or in a mortar to separate fibers.
4. Dilute in water to 1% consistency.

### Forming Sheets

1. Dip mold into pulp; lift horizontally.
2. Shake side-to-side to interlock fibers.
3. Drain; couch sheet onto felt.
4. Stack sheets between felts.

### Pressing & Drying

1. Press stack to remove water.
2. Hang sheets to dry on a line or board.
3. Dried sheets are brittle; size them.

### Sizing

1. Dip in warm gelatin (3%) or starch solution.
2. Dry. Sized paper resists ink bleed.

### Recycled Paper

1. Tear waste paper; soak 24 hours.
2. Blend in water; strain.
3. Proceed as above; fibers are shorter — mixed sheets may be weaker.

## Safety Notes

- Alkaline pulp can irritate skin — wear gloves for long sessions.
- Mold growth on drying sheets is possible in humid climates; dry thoroughly.
- Do not use treated or painted wood scraps for pulp.

title: Salt Production and Iodization
yield: 20-30 kg of salt per 1,000 L of seawater, depending on salinity and recovery
season: Dry, sunny, windy season for solar evaporation
storage: Keep dry in a sealed container; salt keeps indefinitely
hazards: Iodine deficiency if salt is not iodized
materialsRequired: Iodine or iodized salt for fortification

sources.title: US Army FM 21-10 Water and Salt

body:
## Overview

Salt preserves food, supports health, and trades well. Seawater contains about
3.5% salt, so 1,000 L can yield roughly 20-30 kg of usable salt after losses.
Solar evaporation is cheapest in hot, dry, windy places; boiling works in wet
climates but consumes fuel. Iodization prevents goitre and cretinism, so it is
part of making salt safe and useful.

## Prerequisites

- Access to clean seawater, brine springs, or rock salt
- A flat, sun-exposed site or fuel for boiling

## Materials & Tools

- Clean seawater or brine
- Shallow evaporation pans lined with clay or concrete
- Filter cloth
- Fuel and a boiling vessel for wet climates
- Iodine or iodized salt for fortification
- Sealed storage containers

## Procedure

### 1. Source and filter

1. Collect seawater away from sewage outfalls, harbours, and industrial
   discharges.
2. Let the water settle, then filter through cloth to remove sand and debris.
3. Concentrate brine in a pre-evaporation pan before the final crystallizer.
4. Do not use lead pipes or galvanized containers for acidic brine.

### 2. Evaporate

1. Fill shallow pans and expose them to sun and wind.
2. Stir occasionally and top up with fresh brine as it evaporates.
3. Remove scum and dirt as they collect.
4. In wet weather, boil brine in a clean vessel, skimming the surface.

### 3. Harvest and wash

1. Scrape crystals before the brine dries completely; bitter salts remain in
   the liquid.
2. Drain the salt in a cloth-lined basket.
3. Wash briefly with clean saturated brine, not fresh water, to remove
   impurities without dissolving the product.
4. Dry in the sun or a warm, ventilated place.

### 4. Iodize and store

1. Add iodine at the locally recommended rate, or blend with iodized salt.
2. Mix thoroughly and test if a kit is available.
3. Pack in dry, sealed containers; moisture makes salt cake and corrodes metal.
4. Label the batch and keep it away from fuel, pesticides, and animals.

## Safety Notes

- **Yellow hazard:** Boiling brine causes severe burns. Use long handles,
  gloves, and eye protection.
- Contaminated seawater can produce salt laced with heavy metals or pathogens.
- Salt production is dehydrating work; drink water and rest in shade.
- Do not rely on uniodized salt alone in regions where iodine deficiency is
  common.

title: Community Food Security Planning
season: Year-round; review before planting and before winter
storage: Keep at least 3 months of staple reserves where storage allows
hazards: Dependency on a single crop or supplier
body:
## Overview

Food security is not only how much a community grows; it is whether every
household can get enough safe, nutritious food through the year. A plan maps
production, stores, gaps, and vulnerable households, then sets reserves and
distribution rules before a crisis. The target is at least three months of
staple reserves where storage allows.

## Prerequisites

- Community organizing
- Basic record keeping

## Materials & Tools

- Household food survey forms
- Maps and records
- Scales and calculators
- Storage inventory sheets
- Seed stock
- Distribution lists and a notice board

## Procedure

### 1. Assess the situation

1. Survey households for stores, income, garden capacity, and dietary needs.
2. Map local production, wild foods, markets, and storage.
3. Identify vulnerable groups: children, pregnant women, elders, disabled
   people, and households without land.
4. Estimate the lean season and the size of the gap.

### 2. Set reserves and priorities

1. Agree a target reserve, such as three months of staples per household.
2. Prioritise diverse, storable foods rather than a single crop.
3. Set clear eligibility and distribution rules before reserves are needed.
4. Protect seed stock separately from eating stock.

### 3. Build and store

1. Support household and communal storage that is dry, cool, and pest-proof.
2. Promote gardens, small livestock, and food preservation.
3. Organise shared tools, threshing, and storage to reduce costs.
4. Record all stock movements and check for spoilage monthly.

### 4. Distribute and review

1. Distribute through trusted local institutions with public records.
2. Target the most vulnerable first; avoid giving to the loudest voices.
3. Review the plan before planting and before winter.
4. Adjust for failed harvests, price changes, and new arrivals.

## Safety Notes

- **Green hazard:** The main risks are social, not physical. Unequal access and
  corruption can cause malnutrition even when food exists.
- Never distribute mouldy or expired food; it can cause acute poisoning.
- Keep distribution peaceful and transparent; publish the rules and amounts.
- Respect dignity and privacy when identifying vulnerable households.

title: Community Organizing
body:
## Overview

Communities solve problems when they organize. Mapping assets, building teams, and acting on shared goals turn scattered individuals into capable groups.

## Prerequisites

- None

## Materials & Tools

- List of members and skills
- Meeting schedule
- Shared task board

## Procedure

### Map & Connect

1. List people, skills, and resources.
2. Identify leaders and trusted connectors.

### Act

1. Choose a concrete, winnable goal.
2. Assign roles, set dates, and review progress.

## Safety Notes

- Include marginalized members; distributed leadership resists burnout.

title: Conflict Resolution
body:
## Overview

Unresolved conflict destroys communities. Mediation that addresses interests, not positions, restores relationships and prevents violence.

## Prerequisites

- None

## Materials & Tools

- Neutral meeting space
- Trained mediators
- Written agreement form

## Procedure

### Mediation

1. Separate parties to cool emotions if needed.
2. Have each side state interests without interruption.
3. Brainstorm options and select a mutually acceptable solution.

### Restoration

1. Agree on restitution or repair.
2. Record the agreement and follow up.

## Safety Notes

- Separate parties where violence is likely; involve the community for safety.

title: Consensus Decision-Making
body:
## Overview

Consensus builds decisions that people will uphold. A clear process separates proposal, discussion, objections, and consent.

## Prerequisites

- None

## Materials & Tools

- Facilitator
- Note-taker
- Agenda

## Procedure

### Proposal & Discussion

1. State the proposal clearly and its rationale.
2. Clarify questions before opinions.

### Objections & Consent

1. Seek principled objections, not vetoes for preference.
2. Amend to address concerns; test for consent.
3. Fall back to a vote only when consensus fails repeatedly.

## Safety Notes

- Protect minority voices; prevent domination by the loudest.

title: Constitution Drafting
body:
## Overview

A constitution fixes the structure of governance, rights, and limits of power. Short, clear, and amendable texts endure best.

## Prerequisites

- Legal Frameworks

## Materials & Tools

- Drafting committee
- Records of debate
- Ratification process

## Procedure

### Draft

1. State purpose, rights, and structure of government.
2. Define amendment and review procedures.

### Ratify

1. Debate publicly and record objections.
2. Adopt by broad consent and publish the text.

## Safety Notes

- Require supermajority for amendment to protect stability.

title: Disaster Preparedness
yield: A practiced community plan with hazard maps, roles, shelters, caches, and drill records
season: Review before seasonal hazards such as floods, wildfires, and storms
storage: Rotate water, food, batteries, and medicines before expiry; keep plans in multiple places
hazards: Panic and traffic during drills or evacuations
Contaminated water and disease after floods
False confidence from an unpracticed plan
lifespan: Review the plan yearly and after every real event
maintenance: Drill twice a year, audit caches quarterly, and update contacts monthly
limits: Not a substitute for trained emergency services
Do not trigger false alarms without coordination
Plans must include people with disabilities, animals, and non-drivers
body:
## Overview

Preparedness is a cycle: understand the hazards, reduce the risks, plan the
response, practice it, and update it. A community plan works when people know
their roles, shelters are reachable, and supplies are stored where they can be
found. A plan written by outsiders and never practiced is worse than no plan
because it creates false confidence.

## Prerequisites

- A map of the community and surrounding hazards
- Agreement on who leads and how decisions are made

## Materials & Tools

- Hazard and resource map
- Contact list and radio plan
- Emergency supply caches
- Shelter signs and route markers
- First aid and triage kits
- Registration and family reunification forms
- Drill log and after-action notes

## Procedure

### 1. Map hazards and resources

1. Mark flood zones, landslide slopes, fire risk, industrial sites, and safe
   high ground.
2. Locate water, food stores, clinics, shelters, and alternative routes.
3. List vulnerable people: older adults, people with disabilities, pregnant
   women, children, and those without transport.
4. Identify likely secondary hazards such as contaminated water or downed
   power lines.

### 2. Assign roles and thresholds

1. Name a coordinator, deputy, and section leads for shelter, health, logistics,
   and communication.
2. Agree on trigger points for warning, evacuation, and shelter opening.
3. Set a communication tree and a fallback meeting place.
4. Write the plan in plain language and translate it into local languages.

### 3. Prepare supplies and shelters

1. Stock water, food, first aid, lighting, tools, and sanitation for at least
   three days.
2. Inspect shelters for access, ventilation, water, and structural safety.
3. Store supplies in multiple locations and rotate them before expiry.
4. Mark routes and shelters so they are visible at night.

### 4. Drill and improve

1. Run a tabletop exercise, then a short field drill.
2. Time the warning, evacuation, and shelter setup; note bottlenecks.
3. Ask participants what failed and assign fixes with dates.
4. Review the plan yearly and after every real event.

## Safety Notes

- **Yellow hazard:** Drills can cause traffic, falls, and panic. Tell
  participants what is happening and keep routes clear.
- Do not create false alarms; coordinate with local authorities.
- Shelters need separate sanitation, safe water, and protection from violence.
- People with disabilities and animals need explicit transport and access plans.

title: Economics
body:
## Overview

Economics allocates scarce resources. Tracking production, storage, and exchange prevents both shortage and waste.

## Prerequisites

- None

## Materials & Tools

- Ledger
- Weights and measures
- Market space

## Procedure

### Accounting

1. Record production, consumption, and stores.
2. Balance the books regularly.

### Exchange

1. Set fair prices or exchange rates.
2. Maintain trust through standard measures and honest weights.

## Safety Notes

- Prevent hoarding and fraud through transparent records.

title: Ethics
body:
## Overview

Ethics guides hard choices, especially triage and resource allocation. Shared principles make decisions defensible and reduce resentment.

## Prerequisites

- None

## Materials & Tools

- Discussion circle
- Case examples
- Written principles

## Procedure

### Principles

1. Agree on core values: dignity, fairness, non-harm, stewardship.
2. Apply consistently across members.

### Triage

1. Prioritize by urgency and likelihood of benefit.
2. Document reasoning to maintain trust.

## Safety Notes

- Protect the vulnerable; avoid decisions made from fear or bias.

title: Games
body:
## Overview

Games transmit strategy, math, and social skills. They are played for joy,
teaching, and community bonding.

## Prerequisites

- None

## Materials & Tools

- Dice, stones, sticks, boards, cards
- Two or more players

## Procedure

### Dice

- **Knucklebones:** animal ankle bones.
- **Cubical dice:** carved from wood, bone, or clay.
- **Games:** craps, yatzy, liars' dice.

### Mancala

1. Board with 2 rows of 6 pits + 2 stores.
2. Each pit starts with 4 stones.
3. Sow stones counter-clockwise.
4. Capture opponent's stones.
5. Win by accumulating the most.

### Tigers & Goats

1. 4 tigers vs 20 goats on a 5×5 grid.
2. Goats block; tigers jump to capture.
3. Tigers win by eating 5 goats.
4. Goats win by blocking all tigers.

### Chess

1. 8×8 board.
2. Each side: 8 pawns, 2 rooks, 2 knights, 2 bishops, 1 queen, 1 king.
3. Objective: checkmate the king.
4. Teaches strategy, patience, foresight.

### Go

1. 19×19 board (or 13×13, 9×9 for beginners).
2. Players place black/white stones alternately.
3. Surround territory to capture.
4. Objective: control more territory than opponent.
5. Oldest continuously-played board game.

### Playing Cards

1. 52-card deck (4 suits × 13 ranks).
2. Games: poker, bridge, whist, rummy.
3. Card games teach probability.

### The Game of Life (Simulation)

1. Board with life path.
2. Spin to advance.
3. Choices: career, family, wealth.
4. Teaches consequences.

### Physical Games

- Tag, hide-and-seek, races.
- Wrestling, tug-of-war.
- Ball games: soccer, catch, juggling.

### Teaching Games

- Counting games for children.
- Memory games.
- Strategy games for teens.

### Gambling

- Historically common but harmful.
- If played, keep stakes symbolic.
- Never gamble essentials.

## Safety Notes

- Green — but gambling addiction destroys families. Avoid real stakes.
- Physical games risk injury; warm up and play fairly.
- Chess and Go can become obsessive; balance.

title: Legal Frameworks
body:
## Overview

Law provides predictable rules for property, harm, and disputes. A simple, published, and evenly applied code is better than an elaborate but hidden one.

## Prerequisites

- Conflict Resolution

## Materials & Tools

- Written code
- Court or hearing space
- Records

## Procedure

### Drafting

1. Define rights, duties, and offences in plain language.
2. Set proportionate penalties and fair procedures.

### Adjudication

1. Hear both sides with evidence.
2. Decide openly and record the reasoning.
3. Provide appeal to a higher body.

## Safety Notes

- Guard against bias; require recusal where a judge has a stake.

title: Trade & Barter
body:
## Overview

Barter and local exchange move goods without money. Fair terms, standard measures, and reputation keep trade flowing and prevent exploitation.

## Prerequisites

- Economics

## Materials & Tools

- Goods to trade
- Standard weights and measures
- Market rules

## Procedure

### Negotiate

1. Know the value of what you offer and seek.
2. Agree terms before exchanging, ideally with witnesses.

### Local Currency

1. Issue scrip or tally sticks backed by real goods or labor.
2. Track balances to prevent inflation.

## Safety Notes

- Prevent fraud with standard measures and public records.

title: Water Governance
yield: A functioning water committee with written rules, a transparent tariff, and a maintenance fund
season: Establish before the dry season and review after every major repair
storage: Keep cash books, minutes, and maintenance logs in a locked, dry place
hazards: Conflict over access and unpaid fees
Capture of the committee by one family or faction

resourceBudget.batch: one village water point serving 500 users

lifespan: Rules remain workable for 2-3 years before a full review
maintenance: Meet monthly, post accounts, and audit the fund twice a year
limits: Not legal advice; confirm water rights and bylaws locally
Do not deny water to vulnerable households without a written hardship process
Customary and formal rights may overlap and must be reconciled
body:
## Overview

A water point lasts when a community agrees who may use it, who maintains it,
who pays, and how disputes are settled. Governance is not a document on a shelf;
it is a monthly meeting, a visible account, and a maintenance fund. Without
those, pumps break and the poorest households lose access first.

## Prerequisites

- A functioning water source or storage system
- A trusted group willing to serve on a committee

## Materials & Tools

- Written rules and a map of the system
- Membership and user register
- Cash book, receipts, and a lockbox
- Maintenance log and spare-parts list
- Notice board
- Meeting space and minutes book

## Procedure

### 1. Define the water system and users

1. Map the source, storage, pipes, taps, and private connections.
2. List households, institutions, livestock, and businesses that use the system.
3. Identify who owns the land and who holds customary or legal water rights.
4. Agree on the boundaries of the service area.

### 2. Set rules and responsibilities

1. Elect a committee with clear terms, including women and minority users.
2. Write rules for access, queueing, livestock, gardening, and private
   connections.
3. Assign maintenance tasks and name who can authorize repairs.
4. Set penalties for damage, theft, and pollution that are fair and enforceable.

### 3. Set a tariff and maintenance fund

1. Choose a fee that covers routine service, spare parts, and a reserve.
2. Decide whether households, institutions, and businesses pay differently.
3. Issue receipts, keep a cash book, and post a monthly summary.
4. Audit the account publicly at least twice a year.

### 4. Meet, repair, and resolve disputes

1. Hold a regular community meeting with minutes.
2. Log every repair, cost, and downtime; review the log monthly.
3. Resolve disputes through a defined process before they escalate.
4. Review the rules every two to three years or after a major failure.

## Safety Notes

- **Green hazard:** Governance work is low physical risk but can generate
  conflict. Hold meetings in public, keep records, and avoid capture by one
  family or faction.
- Do not cut off water to households that cannot pay without a written
  hardship process.
- Protect the source from contamination and keep sanitation away from intakes.
- This is a governance guide, not legal advice; confirm water rights locally.

title: Basic First Aid
body:
## Overview

Field first aid prioritizes: airway, breathing, circulation (ABC), then
bleeding control, then shock prevention. Definitive care is in
[Health](../health/README.md).

## Prerequisites

- None

## Materials & Tools

- Clean cloth
- Boiled water
- Improvised splints
- Honey (antimicrobial)

## Procedure

### ABC Check

1. **Airway:** tilt head back, lift chin. Clear obstructions.
2. **Breathing:** look, listen, feel for 10 seconds.
3. **Circulation:** check carotid pulse.

### CPR (Adult)

1. 30 chest compressions (5–6 cm deep) at 100–120/min.
2. 2 rescue breaths.
3. Repeat. Continue until help arrives or the person revives.

### Bleeding Control

1. Apply direct pressure with a clean cloth.
2. Add layers without removing the first.
3. If severe, apply a tourniquet 5–7 cm above the wound.
4. Note tourniquet time; do not remove in the field.

### Fracture Splinting

1. Immobilize joints above and below the fracture.
2. Pad the splint.
3. Check distal pulse before and after.

### Burn Care

1. Cool with clean running water for 20 minutes.
2. Cover with a clean, non-stick dressing.
3. Do not pop blisters.
4. Do not apply butter, oil, or ice.

### Shock Prevention

1. Lay the person flat; raise legs 30 cm.
2. Keep warm.
3. Give nothing by mouth if unconscious.

## Safety Notes

- **Red hazard:** Do not move someone with a suspected spinal injury unless in immediate danger.
- Improper CPR can cause rib fractures; correct hand placement matters.
- Tourniquets can cause tissue death; use only for life-threatening bleeding.

title: Cold Exposure and Hypothermia
season: Cold, wet, or windy conditions; risk rises at night and after rain
hazards: Rewarming burns or alcohol-related blood vessel dilation

sources.title: US Army FM 21-10 Cold Weather Casualty Care

body:
## Overview

Cold kills by lowering the body's core temperature. Wet clothing, wind, and
exhaustion accelerate heat loss far faster than cold air alone. Hypothermia
begins with shivering and clumsy hands, progresses to confusion and slurred
speech, and can end in cardiac arrest. The priority is to stop heat loss and
warm the core, not to warm the extremities first.

## Prerequisites

- Emergency shelter
- Fire or another heat source

## Materials & Tools

- Dry insulating layers and a windproof outer layer
- Warm blankets or a sleeping bag
- Fire-starting kit
- Warm, sweet fluids if the person is fully alert
- Emergency shelter or windbreak

## Procedure

### 1. Recognize the condition

1. Look for uncontrolled shivering, numbness, clumsy movement, confusion, or
   drowsiness.
2. Check responsiveness and breathing; treat cardiac arrest with CPR and call
   for help.
3. Handle the person gently; rough movement can trigger an irregular heartbeat
   in severe hypothermia.
4. Assume hypothermia in any wet, exhausted person in cold or windy conditions.

### 2. Stop heat loss

1. Move to shelter, out of wind and rain.
2. Remove wet clothing by cutting it off if necessary; keep the person
   horizontal.
3. Insulate from the ground with mats, packs, or dry branches.
4. Cover the head, neck, and torso; use a vapour barrier if available.

### 3. Warm the core

1. Apply skin-to-skin heat or warm blankets to the chest, neck, and groin.
2. Give warm, sweet drinks only if the person is fully conscious and can
   swallow; never give alcohol.
3. Use a fire or heater to warm the shelter, not to directly roast the skin.
4. Evacuate severe cases; do not attempt vigorous rewarming in the field.

### 4. Manage frostbite

1. Do not rub snow, massage, or walk on frozen feet.
2. Rewarm only when there is no risk of refreezing, using warm water around
   37-39 C.
3. Protect blisters and separate fingers and toes with dry gauze.
4. Seek medical care; frostbite can look harmless before tissue dies.

## Safety Notes

- **Red hazard:** Severe hypothermia can cause cardiac arrest. Handle the
  person gently and evacuate.
- Alcohol increases heat loss and impairs judgement; never use it to warm
  someone.
- Do not apply direct heat to numb skin; burns are common.
- Rewarming a frostbitten limb that may freeze again causes more damage than
  waiting.

title: Edible & Inedible Plants
body:
## Overview

Plants provide calories, vitamins, and medicine — but misidentification kills.
Follow the **Universal Edibility Test** only in true survival situations. When
possible, rely on positive identification.

## Prerequisites

- [Finding Water](finding-water.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Plant samples
- Water for boiling
- Time (test takes 24 hours per plant)

## Procedure

### Positive Identification First

Learn 10–20 plants in your bioregion with absolute certainty before an
emergency. Prioritize:

- Dandelion (all parts edible)
- Plantain (leaves, seeds)
- Cattail (rhizomes, shoots, pollen)
- Clover (leaves, flowers)
- Acorns (leached of tannins)

### Universal Edibility Test (Last Resort)

1. **Separate** the plant into leaves, stem, root, bud, flower.
2. **Smell** each part; discard anything with an almond, peach, or bitter smell.
3. **Skin contact:** rub a small piece on inner wrist; wait 15 minutes.
4. **Lip contact:** place on lips; wait 15 minutes.
5. **Tongue:** place on tongue; wait 15 minutes.
6. **Chew:** chew a small piece and spit; wait 15 minutes.
7. **Swallow:** swallow one small piece; wait 8 hours.
8. If no reaction, eat ¼ cup and wait another 8 hours.

### Dangerous Families (Never Eat Unless Expert)

- Apiaceae (hemlock, water hemlock) — carrot family, deadly
- Solanaceae (nightshade, datura) — many toxic alkaloids
- Euphorbiaceae (spurge) — milky sap burns
- Mushrooms — unless 100% identified, never

### Preparation

- Boil most wild greens twice, discarding water, to remove oxalates and tannins.
- Leach acorns in cold water for 3 days, changing water twice daily.
- Cook cattail rhizomes; peel fibrous outer layer.

## Safety Notes

- **Red hazard:** Misidentification can be fatal within hours.
- Never eat plants with milky sap, umbrella flowers, or three-leaf patterns.
- Never eat mushrooms based on a book or app alone.
- Keep a charcoal slurry on hand in case of poisoning (see [Charcoal Production](../materials/charcoal-production.md)).

title: Emergency Shelter
materialsRequired: Location with natural windbreak (rock, tree, ridge)
body:
## Overview

Exposure kills faster than hunger or thirst. A shelter must address four
threats: wind, rain, cold, and ground conduction. Priority order: insulate
from the ground, block wind, shed rain, retain heat.

## Prerequisites

- None

## Materials & Tools

- Debris (branches, leaves, grass)
- Cordage (see [Rope & Cordage](rope-cordage.md))
- Knife or sharp stone
- Location with natural windbreak (rock, tree, ridge)

## Procedure

### Lean-To

1. Find a ridgepole (3–4 m straight branch).
2. Anchor one end in a tree fork or rock; support the other with a Y-stick.
3. Lean branches against the ridgepole at 45° to form a wall.
4. Cover with leaves, moss, or bark. Layer thickly — 30 cm minimum.
5. Build a fire reflector wall of logs 1 m from the opening.

### Debris Hut

1. Build an A-frame with two forked sticks and a ridgepole.
2. Pile leaves and branches to 1 m thickness on both sides.
3. Fill the interior with dry leaves for insulation.
4. Crawl in feet-first; plug the entrance with a leaf bundle.

### Snow Cave (Winter)

1. Find a drift at least 2 m deep.
2. Dig a tunnel 1 m long, then up into a dome.
3. Smooth the ceiling to prevent dripping.
4. Poke a ventilation hole with a ski pole.
5. Build a sleeping platform 30 cm above the floor.

## Safety Notes

- Never sleep directly on the ground — conduction steals heat 25x faster than air.
- Snow caves require ventilation; CO₂ builds up while sleeping.
- Avoid dead trees overhead (widowmakers).

title: Finding Water
materialsRequired: Solar still materials (plastic sheet, cup, vegetation)
body:
## Overview

Humans die in 3 days without water. Before treating water, you must find it.
Sources ranked by safety: springs > rainwater > flowing streams > lakes >
stagnant pools.

## Prerequisites

- [Water Purification](water-purification.md) (all found water must be treated)

## Materials & Tools

- Container
- Cloth (for pre-filtering)
- Solar still materials (plastic sheet, cup, vegetation)

## Procedure

### Reading the Landscape

1. Follow game trails downhill — they lead to water.
2. Watch for swarms of insects at dusk (water nearby).
3. Look for green vegetation in arid terrain (indicates subsurface water).
4. Dig in dry riverbeds at the outside of bends.

### Solar Still

1. Dig a pit 1 m wide, 60 cm deep.
2. Place a cup in the center.
3. Fill the pit with green vegetation around the cup.
4. Cover with clear plastic; seal edges with soil.
5. Place a small stone at the center above the cup.
6. Collect condensed water after 6–8 hours.

### Vegetation Transpiration Bag

1. Tie a clear plastic bag around a leafy branch of a non-toxic tree.
2. Seal the opening; weight the bottom corner.
3. Collect transpired water after a day.

### Rain Catchment

1. Stretch cloth or plastic to funnel rain into a container.
2. Line large leaves (banana, taro) into a trough.
3. First 10 minutes of rain washes the surface — discard.

## Safety Notes

- **Never drink untreated water** — see [Water Purification](water-purification.md).
- Avoid water with algae blooms, oil sheen, or dead animals upstream.
- Desert plants may hold water but many are toxic; identify before drinking.
- Snow and ice must be melted — eating it causes hypothermia.

title: Making Fire
materialsRequired: Tinder (dry grass, birch bark, char cloth)
Ignition source (one of the methods below)
body:
## Overview

Fire provides warmth, light, cooking, water purification, and protection.
Mastering multiple ignition methods ensures resilience across environments.

## Prerequisites

- None

## Materials & Tools

- Tinder (dry grass, birch bark, char cloth)
- Kindling (small dry twigs)
- Fuel (larger dry wood)
- Ignition source (one of the methods below)

## Procedure

### Method 1: Ferro Rod

1. Scrape magnesium from the rod onto a small pile of tinder.
2. Hold the striker at a 45° angle to the rod.
3. Draw the striker down the rod firmly to create sparks.
4. Direct sparks into the magnesium pile.
5. Once the tinder catches, add kindling gradually.

### Method 2: Bow Drill

1. Carve a fireboard with a shallow depression and a notch.
2. Cut a spindle about 20 cm long, pointed at both ends.
3. Make a bow with a flexible branch and cordage.
4. Use a socket (stone or hardwood) to press the spindle.
5. Saw the bow back and forth with steady pressure.
6. When the notch glows, transfer the ember to tinder.

### Method 3: Flint and Steel

1. Hold the flint at a 45° angle above the tinder.
2. Strike the steel downward against the flint.
3. Catch sparks on char cloth.
4. Blow gently to ignite the tinder.

## Safety Notes

- Never build a fire under overhanging branches.
- Keep a water source or sand nearby.
- Avoid flammable clothing when tending fire.
- Do not leave fires unattended.

title: Rope & Cordage
materialsRequired: Fibrous plants: nettle, hemp, flax, yucca, inner bark of basswood/willow
body:
## Overview

Cordage is a force multiplier — needed for shelter, traps, fire-making, and
construction. Any fibrous plant can become cordage.

## Prerequisites

- None

## Materials & Tools

- Fibrous plants: nettle, hemp, flax, yucca, inner bark of basswood/willow
- Hands

## Procedure

### Extracting Fiber

1. Harvest plant stems at the end of the growing season.
2. Ret in water 1–3 weeks until bark slips easily.
3. Peel fiber strips lengthwise.
4. Dry in shade to prevent brittleness.

### Reverse-Wrap (Two-Strand Twist)

1. Split fiber into two roughly equal strands.
2. Twist strand A clockwise.
3. Wrap strand B counter-clockwise over strand A.
4. Repeat, alternating, keeping tension.
5. Splice in new fiber by overlapping ends and twisting together.

### Three-Strand Braid

1. Anchor three strands.
2. Cross right over middle, then left over middle.
3. Repeat. Stronger and more uniform than two-strand.

### Making Rope from Vines

1. Score a vine with a rock and peel in long strips.
2. Soak in water for flexibility.
3. Braid 3–4 strips together.

## Safety Notes

- Test cordage load before trusting it with weight.
- Nettle requires gloves when harvesting.
- Retting water smells; do it away from camp.

title: Search and Rescue
yield: A documented search sector with clue log, coverage map, and safe patient handover
season: Year-round; search urgency increases in cold, heat, and darkness
storage: Keep search kits packed and maps current; replace batteries every 6 months
hazards: Hypothermia, heat illness, and dehydration in searchers
Violence or hazardous persons at the scene
Loss of situational awareness in darkness

lifespan: Search skills remain usable for about 1 year without practice
maintenance: Practice grid search and radio check-ins quarterly

Do not search alone
Do not move a patient before assessing and stabilizing life threats
